summary:
Legal gender recognition in Andorra rests on the Family Law adopted on 21 July 2022, part of the 2022 Law of the Person and Family, which allows trans people to change the name and gender recorded on legal documents through a simple procedure that requires no medical intervention. The same 2022 reform introduced unified civil marriage.

Non-discrimination protection is set by Law 13/2019 of 15 February 2019, which bars discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression across employment, education, health care, social services, housing and public establishments. Law 14/2019 of 15 February 2019 on the rights of children and adolescents establishes that transgender children must be respected in their gender identity.

The Penal Code provides additional penalties for offences motivated by the victim's sexual orientation, and the wider legal framework indexes hate crime and discrimination provisions. No formal system exists in Andorra to register and classify bias-motivated violence, however, and the principal LGBTI organisation DiversAnd has called for one so that such incidents can be recognised as hate crime. The absence of that machinery indicates the generic hate-crime provisions are not routinely applied to bias incidents.

Andorran police recorded an average of two to three bias-motivated incidents each month during 2025, according to ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2026. DiversAnd flagged incidents around the June Pride celebrations of that year and reported them publicly. The Ministry of Equality implemented equality measures during the same year.

Access to gender-affirming care is not settled. In August 2023 DiversAnd met the Ministry of Health to press for protocols covering puberty blockers and hormone therapy for 16-year-olds, and in some cases for 14-year-olds, following regulatory changes made in 2022. Whether those protocols have since been adopted is not stated in the sources.

Transphobic expression in the media has drawn a public response. A transphobic opinion piece published in El Periòdic d'Andorra on 27 September 2023 was removed from the newspaper's website with a public apology after DiversAnd requested its removal, although the article had already appeared in the print edition.
tangentialFactors:
Andorra's public climate is comparatively open. Public LGBT expression is protected, the first LGBT demonstration was held on 6 September 2002 and the first pride parade followed on 23 June 2003 at Plaça del Poble in Andorra la Vella, organised by the association Som Com Som. DiversAnd was formed in 2019 after Som Com Som ended its work in 2018, and organised a pride parade in June 2019.

The serving head of government, Xavier Espot Zamora, in office since 2019, came out as gay publicly in September 2023, stating "I never hid it". The Ministry of Equality obliges companies operating in the country to maintain protocols against sexual and gender-based harassment, and the Department of Equality launched the short film "#lovingdiversity" on 17 May 2019 to raise online awareness.

Documented violence against LGBT people is historical rather than recent but is not absent from the record: in 2000 a 17-year-old gay man, Nuno Ribeiro, was killed in the country because of his sexual orientation, prompting public outcry, and cases of parents expelling their children from home over their sexual orientation have been reported. Since the 2014 civil union law, adoption has been open to same-sex couples.
localsOnly:
Residents benefit from the education protections in Law 13/2019, which extends non-discrimination cover including gender identity and gender expression to education settings, and from Law 14/2019, which requires that transgender children be respected in their gender identity. Preventing and addressing bullying and discrimination in schools is a stated focus of DiversAnd's work.

The legal document change available under the 2022 Family Law is a domestic procedure for residents updating national identity records; it does not describe how foreign documents are treated. Civil unions remain available alongside the unified civil marriage introduced in 2022.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources do not state whether the gender-affirming care protocols requested from the Ministry of Health in August 2023 have been adopted, nor the age thresholds finally agreed.

Unresolved: the two to three bias-motivated incidents recorded monthly during 2025 are not broken down by motive, so the share directed at trans people specifically is not sourced. No source in the inventory documents a hate-crime prosecution or sentence arising from a bias incident in Andorra.

Not sourced: entry, visa and border-document rules for trans visitors, including how a passport with an amended gender marker is handled on arrival, and whether any screening at entry risks disclosure. Nothing in the inventory addresses facilities, restroom access or partner recognition for visitors.

GayLawNet's Andorra page, which indexes civil unions, discrimination, hate crimes, marriage and trans legal status and sets the age of consent at 16 under Penal Code Article 206, carries a "limited information" marking and should be treated as a partial index rather than a current statement of the law.
